name: Testagen
summary: A Russian dietary-supplement peptide from Khavinson's 'bioregulator' research, promoted for male reproductive health and testosterone; human evidence is one small study by its developers.
what_it_is: Testagen is a short synthetic peptide developed at Vladimir Khavinson's institute in St. Petersburg and listed in Russia as a dietary supplement for men. Its Russian listing describes a peptide complex made from four amino acids: lysine, glutamic acid, aspartic acid and glycine. Its developers say it acts specifically on testicular tissue, supporting sperm production and testosterone, but this rests on their own rat and human studies.

evidence.why: Rat studies and one small randomized study in 48 older men, all reported by the developers in a Russian drug-reference article rather than a peer-reviewed journal.

status_us.label: Not FDA-approved; not on FDA compounding lists
status_us.note: Testagen is not an FDA-approved drug and appears on none of FDA's compounding lists (nominated substances, updated May 2026; safety-risk and withdrawn nominations, April 2026). FDA allows pharmacy compounding only from ingredients that are in an approved drug, meet a USP standard, or are on or under review for its bulk list; in Russia it is listed as a dietary supplement.

benefits.claim: Higher blood testosterone and better sperm count, movement and shape in a small randomized study of 48 men aged 54 to 68 with age-related symptoms
Better well-being and sexual activity reported by men in the same study
Less radiation damage to sperm production and fertility in male rats
Stimulated growth of testicular tissue from young and old rats in lab culture, with no clear effect on brain, heart, liver, kidney or prostate tissue

risks.risk: The developers report no side effects, but no independent human safety data exist
No FDA-approved or pharmacy-compounded version exists, so the identity and purity of products are unverified

avoid_if: Prostate or breast cancer, or another hormone-sensitive condition, unless a clinician is involved
Known fertility problems, unless a fertility specialist is involved

before: Morning total testosterone, with LH and FSH, if low testosterone is the concern
Semen analysis if fertility is the concern
during: Repeat the same tests to see whether anything changed
labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists for Testagen; these are the measures the developers' study tracked.

studies.title: Клинико-экспериментальное изучение пептидного биорегулятора Тестагена (Clinical and experimental study of the peptide bioregulator Testagen)
studies.people: 48 men aged 54 to 68 with age-related (climacteric) symptoms: 27 given Testagen plus standard care, 21 standard care alone
studies.finding: The Testagen group had a significant rise in testosterone and better semen measures, and no side effects were reported. The developers' report gives few details on how the study was run.

ask_your_clinician: Has my testosterone been confirmed low with proper morning tests, and what is causing it?
Are there proven treatments for my symptoms or fertility goals?
Could this affect my fertility tests or any treatment I am on?

notes_for_editor: All human and rat data come from one article by the developers (Khavinson and Ryzhak) in the RLS drug-reference handbook, not a peer-reviewed journal; methods are thin and no independent study was found. The Russian listing names the amino acids (lysine, glutamic acid, aspartic acid, glycine) but not their order; online catalogs call it KEDG (Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly), which has an NLM MeSH record (C560777), but no opened source ties that record to the name Testagen. The RLS article's disclaimer calls it a medicinal product while the RLS register lists it as a dietary supplement; we went with the supplement listing.
